title: Why Are Soviet-Era Planes Still Flying? The An-12 Crash Near Kemerovo, Explained
fb_caption: On the evening of 17 November 2026, a Russian military Antonov An-12 transport plane crashed in an unpopulated area near Kemerovo, Siberia. Russia's Defence Ministry cited a preliminary technical malfunction, and investigators have opened a case. The An-12 first flew in 1957. So why do Cold War designs like it keep flying? Three big reasons: they were built tough, they're cheap to run, and there are few replacements. Plus the trade-off that comes with age. Would you fly on a plane older than your parents? beats.text: On the evening of November 17th, a Russian military Antonov An-12 cargo plane crashed in an unpopulated area near Kemerovo, in Siberia. Russia's Defence Ministry pointed to a preliminary technical malfunction.
Investigators have opened a case. But the An-12 first flew back in 1957. So why are planes designed in the Cold War still flying today? Here are the three big reasons.

One: they were built tough. Soviet cargo planes were designed for short, rough, unpaved airstrips and brutal cold. A high wing keeps the four propellers clear of gravel and snow, and sturdy landing gear handles bumpy ground.

Two: they're cheap. More than twelve hundred An-12s were built, so there are huge stocks of spare parts and mechanics who know them inside out. And an old plane that's already paid for costs far less than a new one.

Three: there are few replacements. New cargo planes are expensive and slow to build, and Western sanctions have made it harder for Russia to get new aircraft and foreign parts. So old fleets keep flying.
But there's a trade-off. Old airframes suffer from metal fatigue and corrosion. Keeping them safe takes more inspections, more repairs, and more maintenance hours every year.
Think of it like a classic car. You can keep it running for decades, but only if you check it constantly and replace parts before they wear out.

Would you fly on a plane that's older than your parents? Tell us in the comments, and send this to someone who loves aviation. Because a design that first flew in 1957 was still flying over Siberia this November.
